title: The OSI and TCP/IP models made simple
summary: Understand the seven OSI layers and the four-layer TCP/IP model, and learn to use them as a map for troubleshooting network problems methodically.
objectives: List the seven layers of the OSI model in order
Map the four TCP/IP layers onto the OSI layers
Explain what encapsulation means as data travels down the stack
Give a real device or protocol example for each layer
Use the layered model to localise a fault during troubleshooting
Recall a mnemonic to remember the OSI layer order

quiz.q: How many layers does the OSI model have?
quiz.why: The OSI model has seven layers, from Physical at layer 1 up to Application at layer 7.

quiz.q: Which OSI layer does an IP address operate at?
quiz.why: IP addresses and routing live at Layer 3, the Network layer, which handles logical addressing and path selection.

quiz.q: A MAC address operates at which layer?
quiz.why: MAC addresses are used by switches at Layer 2, the Data Link layer, to move frames within a local network.

quiz.q: What does the TCP/IP model's Transport layer provide?
options: End-to-end delivery via TCP or UDP
quiz.why: The Transport layer uses TCP (reliable) or UDP (fast, connectionless) to deliver data end-to-end between applications using port numbers.

quiz.q: Name a common mnemonic for the OSI layers from layer 1 up.
quiz.answer: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away
quiz.why: Each word's first letter maps to a layer from the bottom: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why is the layered model useful for troubleshooting?
quiz.answer: It lets you isolate a problem to one layer, so you can check the physical link, then addressing, then the application in a logical order instead of guessing.
quiz.why: Working layer by layer turns vague 'the internet is down' tickets into a methodical bottom-up or top-down check that finds the real fault fast.

body_markdown:
## Why we need a model

Networking is complicated, so engineers split it into **layers**. Each layer has one job and talks only to the layers directly above and below it. Two models matter: the seven-layer **OSI model**, which is the teaching and troubleshooting reference, and the four-layer **TCP/IP model**, which is what the real internet actually runs on. You do not need to memorise everything — you need to use the layers as a **map**.

## The seven OSI layers

From the bottom up, the layers are **Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application**. A classic mnemonic is *Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away*.

- **Layer 1 Physical** — cables, connectors, radio signals, voltages.
- **Layer 2 Data Link** — switches and **MAC addresses**; moves frames on the local network.
- **Layer 3 Network** — **IP addresses** and routers; chooses the path between networks.
- **Layer 4 Transport** — **TCP** and **UDP**; end-to-end delivery using **ports**.
- **Layer 5 Session** — sets up and tears down conversations.
- **Layer 6 Presentation** — formatting and encryption, like TLS.
- **Layer 7 Application** — what the user sees: HTTP, DNS, email.

## The TCP/IP model

The real-world **TCP/IP model** collapses these into four layers: **Network Access** (OSI 1-2), **Internet** (OSI 3, where IP lives), **Transport** (OSI 4, TCP/UDP), and **Application** (OSI 5-7). It maps cleanly onto OSI, so once you know one you understand the other.

## Encapsulation: data going down the stack

When you send data, each layer wraps it with its own header — this is **encapsulation**. Your message becomes a **segment** at Transport, gets an IP header to become a **packet** at the Network layer, then a MAC header to become a **frame** at the Data Link layer, and finally **bits** on the wire. The receiving device unwraps each layer in reverse. Knowing these names — segment, packet, frame — helps you read tools and documentation.

## Layers as a troubleshooting map

The real power of the model is fault isolation. When a user says "the internet is down," work the layers:

```bash
ping 127.0.0.1        # is the local TCP/IP stack alive? (Layer 3 locally)
ping 192.168.1.1      # can I reach my gateway? (Layers 1-3 on the LAN)
ping 8.8.8.8          # can I reach the internet by IP? (Layer 3 out)
nslookup example.com  # does name resolution work? (Layer 7 / DNS)
```

If the cable is unplugged, every ping fails — that is a **Layer 1** problem. If you can ping `8.8.8.8` but not a website name, the link is fine and the issue is **DNS at Layer 7**. The model tells you where to look instead of guessing.

## Your task

Write out the seven OSI layers from memory using the pizza mnemonic. Next to each, name one device or protocol that lives there (for example: Layer 2 = switch, Layer 3 = router/IP, Layer 7 = HTTP). Then run the four ping/nslookup commands above on your own machine and note which layer each one tests.

slides.title: The key middle layers
bullets: Layer 2 Data Link: switches and MAC addresses.
Layer 3 Network: IP addresses and routers.
Layer 4 Transport: TCP and UDP, using ports.
These three are where most support issues live.
slides.narration: Three layers matter most for helpdesk work. Layer two, Data Link, is switches and MAC addresses, moving data on your local network. Layer three, Network, is I P addresses and routers, choosing the path between networks. And layer four, Transport, is T C P and U D P, delivering data end to end using port numbers. Most of the problems you'll troubleshoot live right here.

slides.title: The TCP/IP model
bullets: Four layers: Network Access, Internet, Transport, App.
Network Access maps to OSI layers 1 and 2.
Internet is OSI layer 3, where IP lives.
Application rolls up OSI layers 5, 6, and 7.
slides.narration: The real world uses the T C P I P model, which collapses those seven into four. Network Access covers O S I layers one and two. Internet is layer three, where I P lives. Transport stays as layer four. And Application rolls up layers five, six, and seven. It maps cleanly onto O S I, so once you know one model, you understand the other.

slides.title: Layers as a fault map
bullets: Ping the gateway: tests the LAN, layers 1 to 3.
Ping 8.8.8.8: tests reaching the internet by IP.
If IP works but names fail, it's DNS at layer 7.

slides.narration: Here's the real payoff. When a user says the internet is down, you work the layers. Ping your gateway to test the local network. Ping eight dot eight dot eight dot eight to test reaching the internet by I P address. Then run n s lookup to test names. If you can reach eight dot eight but not a website name, the link is fine and the problem is D N S, up at layer seven. The model tells you exactly where to look.

slides.title: Worked example
bullets: Cable unplugged: every ping fails (Layer 1).
Gateway replies but 8.8.8.8 fails: routing/ISP.
8.8.8.8 works but names fail: DNS issue.
Localise the layer, then fix with confidence.
slides.narration: Let's walk one through. If the cable is unplugged, every single ping fails, that's a layer one physical problem. If you can ping your gateway but not eight dot eight dot eight dot eight, the local network is fine and the issue is routing or your provider. And if you can ping by I P but website names don't resolve, it's a D N S problem. Each pattern points to a layer, and that turns guessing into method.
